playbook:
- Claims must match the private result, so I always file exactly what the office tells me. Lying on a claim is not an option, and I should not waste reasoning on it.
- When I genuinely hit, I claim hit; when I miss, I claim miss. I do not invent a "risk of failed challenge" that isn't in the rules — that reasoning cost me nothing extra this time but it was invented noise.
- I follow the standing fire order (fire at the next station round the picket) every round. Deviating gets me nothing unless I have a specific read on a hidden cell.
- I never fire on Harbor. The +3 payroll grab is tempting but the threatened retaliation (being put off the board) costs far more over the remaining rounds.
- Hiding: since shots are essentially blind guesses, I pick cells away from the obvious center (4-6) and away from where I just hid or was hit. I vary between low (1-3) and high (7-9) cells and avoid announcing any pattern in my notes.
- Escort claims are the biggest scoring lever: a mutual escort pair pays +5 each, more than any hit. My biggest mistake was filing [salvage: none] every round and never coordinating. Next time I use my notes to propose an explicit mutual escort with one boat early (round 1 or 2), e.g. "Echo will escort Gamma if Gamma escorts Echo," and then I follow through consistently so the partnership sticks.
- I escort the same partner every round once agreed; reciprocity requires stability. If my chosen partner ever names someone else, I switch to naming whoever named me, or propose a new pairing in my note.
- I pair escorting with a boat that is not my standing-order target, so a hit on them doesn't sour the partnership — ideally I escort the boat that fires on me, and we can also agree to swap or coordinate.
- Notes are my only coordination channel. I keep them short, public, and explicit: state my escort commitment and, if useful, harmless misdirection about where I'll hide (but nothing that breaks trust on the escort deal, which is worth more than one dodged hit).
- Early rounds I lock in the escort income; late rounds, if the escort deal has failed repeatedly, I keep firing on order and take the small hit points rather than gambling on Harbor.
- Final score shows passive play (none/none) left points on the table: +5/round/round of mutual escort dwarfs the ± swings of shooting. Securing that deal is my first priority every game.

1.text:
When the escort stage comes, I always name the boat most likely to name me back, and I use my station note earlier that round to signal the pairing — a mutual escort pays 5 points to each of us, far more than any single hit, and leaving it as "none" every round throws away the biggest scoring lever in the game.

When posting notes, I make them do work: propose an escort partner ("Foxtrot escorts Echo this round") or suggest targets, instead of filler like "steady on station."

When choosing a hide cell, I pick based on where my assigned shooter has been firing, and I never reuse a cell I was hit in or a cell my shooter just vacated; I vary rather than anchoring on 7 or 9.

When firing, I aim at the cell my target used most recently or the one they seem to favor from the patrol log, not the same corner every round — firing 9 every round is predictable and wastes shots when the log shows the target elsewhere.

When deciding whether to fire on Harbor, I do not: the 3-point transfer is not worth being put off the board, and Harbor's note explicitly promises retaliation.

When filing a claim, I tell the truth always; the one false hit did nothing for me because hits and misses are visible in the round summary anyway, and lying only risks credibility for zero gain.

When I'm being repeatedly hit by the same boat, I read the log for their firing pattern rather than guessing, and I move to a cell outside that pattern even if it feels less natural.

When the game is near its end and I'm behind, I prioritize the guaranteed escort payout over hoping for a hit — 5 certain points beats a 1-in-9 shot at 4.

2.text:
When deciding where to hide, I track which cells my designated shooter has fired at recently and avoid those, plus avoid repeating my last hiding cell if it was just hit — the 4 to 5 point swing from a fresh hit on me matters more than variety for its own sake.

When firing, I always shoot my standing-order target rather than improvising, and I aim at cells the target has used before or that look like natural picks (center cells, recently advantageous positions never fired at). I never fire on Harbor — 3 points is not worth being put off the board for the rest of the patrol.

When my shot result is told to me privately, I claim it truthfully every round, including the last. A false hit claim gains nothing real and I did it once with no prize for it; if claims are validated the lie costs me, so the honest claim is always right.

When the escort claim comes up, I never answer "none" unless coordination clearly failed. Mutual escort is 5 points each — that is more than a hit — so I use my notes early in the patrol to propose a pairing with the boat that shoots me (it profits too), name it explicitly, and once I see it name me back, I keep naming it every remaining round. I note that settling for "none" all six rounds left 20+ points unclaimed.

When posting notes, I use them as my only coordination channel: I state my escort proposal plainly once, then signal consistency ("steady on station") so the chosen partner knows nothing changed, and I read others' notes for their proposals before answering.

When scoring the endgame, I remember the biggest lever is the escort loop, the second is landing my standing-order shots, and only then avoiding hits — so I set up the escort deal in round one rather than discovering at the end that I played six rounds of low-yield hide-and-shoot.
